The method reduces the 3D distance calculation to a 2D problem by exploiting rotational symmetry around the cone's axis [S4, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly describes the method for calculating the signed distance to a cone. It states that the point `p` is projected onto the XZ plane to get the radius, and then a 2D point `q` is constructed using this radius and the Y coordinate (`q = Vec2(Vec2(p.x, p.z).length(), p.y)`). This transformation effectively reduces the 3D problem to a 2D cross-section problem. The subsequent calculations (defining tip, base, vectors, and distances) are all performed in this 2D space. This reduction is possible because the cone possesses rotational symmetry around its axis (the Y-axis), meaning the distance depends only on the radial distance from the axis and the height, not the azimuthal angle.
